issues.legal_issue: A court with jurisdiction over a suit for possession may also determine an incidental claim for compensation for use and occupation until possession is delivered.
material_facts: The landlords sued the tenant and the person to whom the tenant had sublet the premises for possession.
The landlords also sought compensation for use and occupation of the premises until vacant possession was delivered.
issues.conclusion: The suit was one for possession, and the claim for compensation was incidental and ancillary to that claim; the court's jurisdiction over possession extended to directions for payment of mesne profits until delivery of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the Small Causes Court had jurisdiction over a suit concerning possession. Jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession also empowered the court to direct payment of mesne profits until possession was delivered, as an integral part of the possession decree. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.

predicates.possession_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking possession of premises from a tenant and an occupant claiming through the tenant.
predicates.compensation_claim_incidental: The landlord sought compensation for use and occupation only as an incident of the claim for possession, including for the period until possession was delivered.

issues.definition: When a landlord's suit seeks possession and the related compensation claim is incidental to that relief, the court deciding possession can also determine the incidental compensation claim.

issues.legal_issue: The court given exclusive jurisdiction over landlord-tenant possession suits may decide a claim or question arising under the rent-control law concerning a subtenant joined in the suit.
material_facts: The landlords sued the tenant for possession of premises to which the relevant part of the rent-control law applied.
The tenant had sublet the premises, and the landlords challenged the subtenant's entitlement to protection under the Act.
The subtenant disputed the Small Causes Court's jurisdiction because it was not itself a tenant of the landlords.
issues.conclusion: Section 28 empowered the Small Causes Court not only to hear the landlord-tenant possession suit but also to deal with a claim or question arising under the Act, including the question concerning the subtenant's rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, gives the Small Causes Court jurisdiction over landlord-tenant suits relating to rent or possession and over claims or questions arising out of the Act or its provisions. The phrase covering any such claim or question is not confined to disputes between landlord and tenant; once a qualifying landlord-tenant suit is before the court, it may determine a properly raised question under the Act. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.

predicates.landlord_tenant_possession_suit: A landlord sued a tenant for possession of premises covered by the rent-control regime.
predicates.subtenant_rights_question_arises_under_r: The suit raised a question about whether a person to whom the tenant had sublet the premises was entitled to protection under the rent-control regime.

issues.definition: If a landlord brings a covered possession suit against a tenant and the suit raises a rent-protection question about a subtenant, the court hearing the suit can decide that question.

issues.legal_issue: Joining a person claiming through a tenant as a proper party to an ejectment suit does not change the suit's character or remove it from the court's statutory jurisdiction.
material_facts: The landlords brought an ejectment suit against the tenant and the subtenant, who claimed through the tenant.
The subtenant was joined so that the dispute about the landlords' right to possession and the subtenant's claimed protection could be determined in that person's presence.
issues.conclusion: Although the subtenant was not a necessary party, the subtenant was a proper party, and joining that party did not alter the character of the suit or take it outside section 28.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, governs the qualifying landlord-tenant suit. Under the ordinary law, a possession decree against a tenant binds a person claiming under or through that tenant even if that person is not joined; such a person may nevertheless be joined as a proper party to contest the landlord's entitlement to possession and seek any available statutory protection. Joinder of a proper party does not change the suit's character or defeat the court's jurisdiction. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.

predicates.landlord_tenant_ejectment_suit: A landlord brought an ejectment suit against a tenant seeking possession of premises covered by the relevant statutory jurisdiction.
predicates.claimant_through_tenant_joined_as_party: A person claiming through the tenant was joined so that the person's position concerning possession or statutory protection could be considered in the suit.

issues.definition: When a person claiming through a tenant is joined in a covered landlord-tenant ejectment suit, that joinder does not remove the suit from the court's statutory jurisdiction.
